terms.brief: The Python/PyTorch environment the software runs on
terms.detail: The synthesis engine runs on Python with PyTorch. It is not part of the installer; on first launch the matching build is downloaded for your graphics card.
The first of GPT-SoVITS’s two stages. It turns text into a sequence of semantic tokens, which is what decides phrasing, stress and intonation. In a character pack this is the .ckpt file.

The second of the two stages. It turns semantic tokens back into a waveform, and it is what carries the timbre. In a character pack this is the .pth file. The two weight files belong together — a mismatched pair produces noise.

terms.brief: The few seconds that set who this sounds like
terms.detail: A short real recording of the character, played to the model at synthesis time. Timbre, pace and mood all follow it, so a different reference makes the same text read differently. Three to ten seconds of clean audio works best.

terms.brief: Exactly what the reference audio says
terms.detail: The transcript of the reference audio. It has to match the recording word for word — a mismatch misleads the model about pronunciation and the result drifts. Character packs carry it in their .list annotations, so you rarely type it yourself.

terms.brief: The dataset index: path, speaker, language, text
terms.detail: GPT-SoVITS’s dataset format — one line per clip: audio path | speaker | language | text. Proofread it on the annotation page before training: every line whose text does not match its audio ends up as a pronunciation fault in the model.

terms.brief: Which language’s rules turn text into sounds
terms.detail: It governs pronunciation, not the character. For text that mixes languages, choose the mixed mode and let the engine decide segment by segment. The classic symptom of the wrong setting is English words read as if they were pinyin.

terms.brief: How long text is broken into pieces before synthesis
terms.detail: The model handles about a sentence at a time, so longer text has to be split first. Splitting on punctuation sounds most natural; splitting by length is more even and suits text without punctuation. Splitting too finely leaves the intonation disjointed between pieces.

terms.brief: Overall faster or slower; 1.0 is unchanged
terms.detail: Applied to the finished audio rather than by re-synthesising, so it never changes how a line is read. Large adjustments sound audibly sped up; 0.8 to 1.2 is the usual range.

terms.brief: How many of the likeliest tokens each step may choose from
terms.detail: Lower is more conservative: steady but flat delivery. Higher lets the model vary its intonation, at the cost of more mistakes. The default of 15 rarely needs changing.

terms.brief: How much the delivery is allowed to vary
terms.detail: Lower is more predictable — the same text reads almost identically every time. Higher is more improvised, with wider emotional range but muddier articulation. Default 1.0.

s.mainGpuTip:
With more than one NVIDIA card, choose which one does the work.
The engine defaults to the lowest-numbered card, which on a machine holding both a 5060 and a 5090 is often not the faster one.
A change applies from the next synthesis or training run.
If a task then refuses to start, or reports insufficient VRAM, set this back to Automatic: when the chosen index does not match what the driver actually enumerates, the engine falls back for want of a card it can find.
s.computeBackendTip:
The device the engine is actually computing on.
The backend is chosen automatically: CUDA when available, CPU otherwise. On CPU, synthesis is much slower; on some machines a virtual display adapter gets picked and the engine then reports insufficient VRAM.
If what you see here is not what you expect, check the main graphics card setting and your display driver.

help.title: Help
help.subtitle: Everything from setup to training. Sections are deep-linkable from within the app.
help.frQ1: What should I do on first launch?
help.frA1: The app detects your GPU and provisions the compute runtime automatically (about 6GB for the NVIDIA build, smaller for CPU). Keep a network connection; this happens only once.
help.frQ2: Where do base models come from?
help.frA2: Synthesis needs pretrained assets such as HuBERT, text features and the GPT base model. The app prompts automatically on first use; you can also fetch them under Plaza → Downloads.
help.frQ3: How do I install a character pack?
help.frA3: Open Library → Import and pick a .zip pack. Installed characters appear on Home and in the Synthesize page.
help.packQ1: What is inside a character pack?
help.packA1: A SoVITS timbre model, a GPT prosody model, a reference set (.list annotations), plus cover art and recommended parameters — packaged as one zip.
help.packQ2: What does the reference audio do?
help.packA2: GPT-SoVITS is few-shot cloning: the model imitates the delivery of the selected reference clip. Switching references changes emotion and pacing.
help.packQ3: Can I package my own trained model?
help.packA3: Yes. After training completes, the Train page offers one-click packaging; existing library models can also be exported as shareable packs.
help.synthQ1: Why doesn't the output match the expected character?
help.synthA1: Make sure the reference comes from the target character's annotations and that text language matches (or use auto). For cross-lingual text prefer a same-language reference.
help.synthQ2: Output loops or breaks up. What should I adjust?
help.synthA2: Raise repetition_penalty or lower temperature for loops; lower top_k for broken or missing syllables. Compare with the same text after each tweak.
help.synthA3: With streaming on, the first audio chunk returns before the whole utterance finishes, cutting perceived latency on long texts. Turn it off for export-grade takes.
help.synthA4: Text is segmented semantically and queued automatically. Batch tasks can be interrupted and resumed.
help.trainQ1: What do I need to train a character?
help.trainA1: Prepare 5+ minutes of music-free, level-consistent speech. Separate vocals and de-noise first if the source is songs or reverberant recordings.
help.trainA2: Use the built-in ASR labeling on sliced clips, then proofread; community-standard .list files can be imported directly.
help.trainQ3: How do I use a finished model?
help.trainA3: Trained models register into your local library automatically and are immediately usable in Synthesize; they can be packaged for the Plaza.
help.listA1: Four pipe-separated columns per line: path|speaker|language|text, e.g. audios/demo.wav|Alice|EN|Hello world. Paths are relative to the pack root.
help.listA2: ZH, JA, EN, KO, YUE. Annotations may be split per language, e.g. name_JP.list alongside name_ZH.list.
help.listQ3: How much does annotation quality matter?
help.listA3: Transcripts are the foundation of quality; bad labels hurt both timbre and prosody. Proofread before training, focusing on polyphones and number readings.
help.faqQ1: Can I use it without an NVIDIA GPU?
help.faqA1: Yes. The app falls back to CPU inference — slower but fully functional. 8GB+ RAM recommended for synthesis; NVIDIA GPUs strongly recommended for training.
help.faqQ2: Can models of different versions be mixed?
help.faqA2: No. v1 / v2 / v2Pro / v2ProPlus / v4 differ in base models and architecture. Version mismatches are detected and reported at load time.
help.faqA3: The synth page manages loaded models with LRU eviction. If still tight, disable streaming, shorten batch length, or use a lighter version.
help.faqQ4: How do I share a character?
help.faqA4: Use Library → Export pack, then submit the zip to the community Plaza. After review it becomes one-click installable for everyone.
